message.content:
In computer‑vision pipelines, “purple” isn’t a special semantic concept on its own—it’s simply one of many RGB values that can be used to encode information.  Practically, purple is often chosen as a **visual cue** because it stands out against common backgrounds (white, black, gray) and is distinct from the primary colors used for other classes.  

Typical uses include:

| Context | Why purple is chosen |
|---------|----------------------|
| **Semantic segmentation masks** | Each class is assigned a unique color; purple is one of the palette entries that is easily distinguishable from red, green, blue, yellow, etc. |
| **Bounding‑box annotations** | Purple lines or outlines help separate objects from the usual red/green/blue annotation styles. |
| **Heat‑maps / saliency maps** | Purple can be part of a colormap that ranges from cool (blue) to warm (red), with purple representing intermediate values. |
| **Data augmentation** | Randomly recoloring objects to purple can test model robustness to color changes. |

So, in computer vision, purple is mainly a **visual marker**—a convenient, high‑contrast color used to label or highlight specific classes, objects, or regions in images and visualizations.
